title: Verifying Identities
learningObjective: Symbolically verify identities by using various trig identities.

faqs.question: What does it mean to "verify" or "prove" an identity?
faqs.answer:
It means showing, step by step, that the two sides are equal for every angle. You start with the expression on one side and use algebra and known identities to transform it, one justified step at a time, until it becomes the expression on the other side. Think of it as a simplification problem with a known destination.

Verifying "cos θ + sin θ tan θ = sec θ": every line changes only the left side, with a reason at each step, until it becomes the right side.

faqs.question: Why can't I treat an identity like an equation (add to, multiply, or cross-multiply both sides)?
faqs.answer:
When you solve an equation, doing the same thing to both sides is fine because you start by assuming the two sides are equal. But in a proof, whether the sides are equal is exactly what you're trying to show. Assuming it is circular reasoning. Instead, keep the two sides apart and change only one of them.

A proof shows the sides are equal, so you can't start by assuming they are. Keep the two sides apart and transform just one into the other.

Why it's dangerous

Start with the false statement \( 1 = -1 \). Square both sides and you get \( 1 = 1 \), which looks true.

But the original statement was false, so \"doing the same thing to both sides\" proved nothing.

faqs.question: Which side should I start with?
faqs.answer:
Usually the more complicated side — the one with fractions, squares, or several terms. It's easier to simplify than to build: a busy side gives you plenty to work with, while a simple side gives you nothing to grab. The simpler side is your target, so keep an eye on which functions it contains (faq-10). If you get stuck one way, you can also start from the other side and work toward the first.

Start on the side with more going on — it gives you more to work with — and let the simpler side show you where to aim.

faqs.question: Which identities am I allowed to use?
faqs.answer:
Any identity you already know — that's your toolbox. The ones you'll use most are the reciprocal, quotient, and Pythagorean identities, plus the sum, double-angle, power-reducing, and half-angle formulas from TE1. Know them well enough to recognize them in disguise: for example, \( 1 - \sin^2\theta \) is really \( \cos^2\theta \).

Your toolbox: every step of a proof is either algebra or one of these identities.

faqs.question: What should I try when I'm stuck?
faqs.answer:
Rewrite everything in terms of sine and cosine, then see what simplifies. It's the one move that almost always helps, because tangent, cotangent, secant, and cosecant are all built from sine and cosine. It won't always be the shortest path, but it gets you started.
Worked Example — verify \( \tan\theta\cos\theta = \sin\theta \)

Start with the left side: \( \tan\theta\cos\theta \)

Rewrite tangent: \( = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\cdot\cos\theta \)

Cancel \( \cos\theta \): \( = \sin\theta \), which is the right side.

faqs.question: How do I combine fractions with a common denominator (like cos θ + sin θ tan θ = sec θ)?
faqs.answer:
After rewriting in sine and cosine, treat it like adding fractions in algebra: put every term over the same denominator, add the numerators, then look for a Pythagorean identity in the numerator.
Worked Example — verify \( \cos\theta + \sin\theta\tan\theta = \sec\theta \)

\( \cos\theta + \sin\theta\cdot\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} \)  (rewrite tangent)

\( = \dfrac{\cos^2\theta}{\cos\theta} + \dfrac{\sin^2\theta}{\cos\theta} \)  (common denominator \( \cos\theta \))

\( = \dfrac{\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta}{\cos\theta} = \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta} = \sec\theta \)  (Pythagorean identity, reciprocal identity)

faqs.question: When and how do I split a fraction apart?
faqs.answer:
When the numerator has a sum or difference and the denominator is a single term, splitting into separate fractions lets each piece simplify on its own. Be careful in the other direction: you can split \( \dfrac{a+b}{c} \) into \( \dfrac{a}{c}+\dfrac{b}{c} \), but you can not split \( \dfrac{c}{a+b} \) into \( \dfrac{c}{a}+\dfrac{c}{b} \).
Worked Example — verify \( \dfrac{\tan\theta-\cot\theta}{\sin\theta\cos\theta} = \sec^2\theta - \csc^2\theta \)

\( \dfrac{\tan\theta}{\sin\theta\cos\theta} - \dfrac{\cot\theta}{\sin\theta\cos\theta} \)  (split the fraction)

\( = \dfrac{\sin\theta/\cos\theta}{\sin\theta\cos\theta} - \dfrac{\cos\theta/\sin\theta}{\sin\theta\cos\theta} \)  (rewrite in sine and cosine)

\( = \dfrac{1}{\cos^2\theta} - \dfrac{1}{\sin^2\theta} = \sec^2\theta - \csc^2\theta \)  (simplify each piece, reciprocal identities)

faqs.question: How do I use factoring and a Pythagorean substitution together (like cos²θ/(1 + sin θ) = 1 − sin θ)?
faqs.answer:
Look at what the answer contains. The target has only sine, so turn the cosine into sine with a Pythagorean identity, then factor the numerator as a difference of squares and cancel. Cancel only whole factors, never terms that are being added.
Worked Example — verify \( \dfrac{\cos^2\theta}{1+\sin\theta} = 1-\sin\theta \)

\( \dfrac{\cos^2\theta}{1+\sin\theta} = \dfrac{1-\sin^2\theta}{1+\sin\theta} \)  (Pythagorean identity)

\( = \dfrac{(1-\sin\theta)(1+\sin\theta)}{1+\sin\theta} \)  (difference of squares)

\( = 1-\sin\theta \)  (cancel the common factor \( 1+\sin\theta \))

faqs.question: When do I multiply by a conjugate, and how?
faqs.answer:
When a numerator or denominator is a two-term expression like 1 − sin θ or 1 + cos θ, multiply top and bottom by its conjugate (the same two terms with the sign flipped). That makes a difference of squares, which a Pythagorean identity can turn into a single term. You're multiplying by 1, so the value doesn't change.
Worked Example — verify \( \dfrac{\cos\theta}{1-\sin\theta} = \dfrac{1+\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} \)

\( \dfrac{\cos\theta}{1-\sin\theta}\cdot\dfrac{1+\sin\theta}{1+\sin\theta} = \dfrac{\cos\theta(1+\sin\theta)}{1-\sin^2\theta} \)  (multiply by the conjugate)

\( = \dfrac{\cos\theta(1+\sin\theta)}{\cos^2\theta} \)  (Pythagorean identity in the denominator)

\( = \dfrac{1+\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} \)  (cancel one \( \cos\theta \))

Tip: leave the numerator factored (don't distribute \( \cos\theta \)) so the cancellation stays easy to see.

faqs.question: How do I decide which tool to try first?
faqs.answer:
Scan the more complicated side for what it looks like, then try the matching move. Also keep the target in mind: look at which functions appear on the simpler side and choose identities that lead toward them. If nothing fits, rewrite in sine and cosine.

Match what you see on the more complicated side to a move. Rewriting in sine and cosine is the fallback that almost always gets you moving.

faqs.question: How do I write up a proof so every step is justified?
faqs.answer:
Write one line per move and note what you used beside it: algebra (common denominator, factoring, cancelling, splitting), a reciprocal or quotient identity, or a Pythagorean identity. End by stating that you arrived at the other side.
Worked Example — verify \( \dfrac{\csc\theta-\sin\theta}{\sin\theta\csc\theta} = \csc\theta-\sin\theta \)

1. \( \dfrac{\csc\theta-\sin\theta}{\sin\theta\csc\theta} \)  — start with the left side

2. \( = \dfrac{\csc\theta}{\sin\theta\csc\theta} - \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\sin\theta\csc\theta} \)  — split the fraction (algebra)

3. \( = \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta} - \dfrac{1}{\csc\theta} \)  — cancel common factors (algebra)

4. \( = \csc\theta - \sin\theta \)  — reciprocal identities: \( \tfrac{1}{\sin\theta}=\csc\theta \) and \( \tfrac{1}{\csc\theta}=\sin\theta \)

5. This is the right side, so the identity is verified.

faqs.question: How can I check my work, or tell whether a statement is even an identity?
How does verifying identities use everything from TE1 and earlier?
faqs.answer: Every step is either algebra (fractions, factoring, cancelling) or an identity you already know: the reciprocal and quotient identities, the Pythagorean identities (TE1 faq-2), and the sum, double-angle, power-reducing, and half-angle formulas. When a problem has 2θ, θ/2, or a sum of angles in it, reach for TE1's formulas. Proving identities is a workout for all of them at once.

faqs.question: How does this skill set up TE3 (solving trig equations)?
faqs.answer: Solving a trig equation often starts by rewriting it — turning a mix of functions into a single function, factoring, or replacing a squared term — using exactly the moves you practiced here. The difference is that in TE3 you are allowed to do the same thing to both sides, because you're solving for the angle rather than proving the two sides equal.

faqs.question: Why does proving things this way matter beyond this course?
faqs.answer: Simplifying an expression before you work with it is a core skill in calculus, for example rewriting a trig expression so it can be differentiated or integrated. And the habit of justifying each step without assuming what you're trying to prove is the foundation of mathematical proof in any later course.

guided.title: Understand Why You Can't Treat an Identity Like an Equation
guided.prompt: I'm learning to verify trig identities. Explain why I can't add to or multiply both sides of an identity the way I would with an equation. Then show me a false statement that looks true after I do the same thing to both sides, and ask me to explain what went wrong.

guided.title: Practice Choosing Which Side to Start With
guided.prompt: Give me several trig identities to verify. For each one, don't solve it — ask me which side I would start with and why, and what functions my target expression contains. Then let me try the first two steps and check my reasoning.

guided.title: Practice Common Denominators and Splitting Fractions
guided.prompt: Give me an identity where I need to add fractions with a common denominator, and another where I need to split one fraction into two. Coach me step by step: ask me what to do next and why, and confirm each step before we move on.

guided.title: Practice Factoring, Pythagorean Substitution, and Conjugates
guided.prompt: Give me identities like cos²θ/(1 + sin θ) = 1 − sin θ and cos θ/(1 − sin θ) = (1 + sin θ)/cos θ. For each, ask me whether I should factor, substitute a Pythagorean identity, or multiply by a conjugate, and why. Check my work and make me justify every step.

guided.title: Check Whether a Statement Is Really an Identity
guided.prompt: Give me several trig statements, some that are true identities and some that are not. For each one, ask me to test an angle or sketch both sides to decide. If it's not an identity, help me find an angle that shows it. If it is, coach me through verifying it.

open.prompt: Use the AI tool of your choice. Start by describing what you're confused about or curious about from Section TE2 (Verifying Identities). Ask the AI to help you explore that idea. Share what you learned and what surprised you.
